column4: We estimated locations and H/L in Google Earth using reference points from photos and using map from Smithsonian Global Volcanism site. The photo from that website was used in conjunction with imagery from before (2004) and after (2015) the rockfalls to estimate the source area, best estimate, min and max. The same H and L values and uncertainties were applied to all of the signals in this sequence because individual runout paths for each cannot be separated.

Jackie Caplan-Auerbach (written communication) "The slide began at about 6,500 feet and had a large runout onto the Red Glacier down to about 1200 feet.  Visually, it looks more like a rock slide than a snow avalanche.  These events look like avalanches in that they are emergent, have a prolonged coda, and a broad spectra. If they're avalanches, there are tons of them, so it could be a gradual failure of a portion of the ice cover.  They do not show the precursory seismicity that we've seen in other Iliamna ice avalanches, however."

Caplan-Auerbach and others (2005) observed more than 20 spindle shaped signals associated with South Twin rockfalls, 0.5 to 9 minutes in duration, typically 20-30 minutes between events. Photo from an overflight (included on page 11 of referenced paper) showed they initiated in rock, not ice. The longest deposit dropped 1 km, horizontal travel distance of at least 3km. No precursory seismicity, unlike avalanches that initiate in ice at Iliamna.

This event occurred before all Alaska data was archived at IRIS. The miniseed files for nearby stations was shared by the Alaska Earthquake Center. We have extracted waveforms from all stations within the maximum radius for which seismic waves were observable for this event, up to 600 km maximum, for 5 minutes before the event approximate start time and 5 minutes after the approximate end time. Metadata information for many stations is available at IRIS, but the metadata for the exact time period may or may not be present.

column4: Total volume estimates for this sequence were determined using source area estimates and bedrock landslide values in Larsen and others (2010) with bedrock scar geometry and then divided up between subevents as explained below. Volume_high and Volume_low estimates made by propagating uncertainties in alpha and gamma values (Larsen and others) and standard deviation of source areas (Area_Source_high, Area_source_low, Area_source). Rounded to two significant digits, the volume estimates for the total amount equal 620,000 m3, with a range of 420,000 to 930,000 m3. The total source area best estimate is 36,000 m2, with a possible range of 17,000-42,000 m2. The volume was then divided proportionally between all South Twin events based on amplitudes at station ILS (2.7 km away), using the finding of Norris (1994) who found that simple landslides that followed the same path with the same slope had amplitudes proportional to their volumes.

Raw waveforms from closest stations. Data was demeaned but no other processing was applied. Dashed lines show approximate start and end times of event (from database). Figure generation is automated and there may be artifacts present.

High frequency (1-5 Hz) ground velocity waveforms for station response from closest stations with detections. Dashed lines show approximate start and end times of event (from database). Waveforms are corrected for station response after removing the mean. Figure generation is automated and there may be artifacts present. Clipped waveforms have not been removed before station correction so check raw plots before interpreting high amplitude signals.
Spectrograms of velocity waveforms corrected for station sensitivity from closest stations with detections. Figure generation is automated and there may be artifacts present

Multitaper spectra (same units as Power Spectral Density) of velocity waveforms corrected for station sensitivity from closest stations with detections. Linear trend was removed and a taper was applied before generating spectra. Figure generation is automated and there may be artifacts present. Since station response was not removed to avoid adding artifacts at low frequencies for short and intermediate period stations, the lower frequency amplitudes should be interpreted with care.
